title: Bring Back Chivalry: A Reply to Aaron Renn
gist: Leonard Sax rebuts Aaron Renn's IFS critique, arguing that boys drifting toward the manosphere need a concrete positive model of manhood, and that 'retro' norms like chivalry and being a gentleman are exactly that. He leans on Daniel Cox's Generation Uncoupled (growing mutual distrust between young men and women) and the Boys to Men program's reported 85% drop in discipline referrals.

insights.speaker: Leonard Sax
insights.so_what: Rising mutual distrust between young men and women is a headwind for coupling, marriage and fertility; watch dating/marriage-rate data.

insights.claim: Leonard Sax argues that vague therapeutic advice such as 'understand a person's reality' and 'care about their well-being' does not work with boys; they need a positive, concrete model of manhood to work toward.
insights.speaker: Leonard Sax
insights.so_what: Frames the debate over how institutions should counter manosphere influence: aspirational norms vs. empathy-based messaging.
insights.quote: We must provide a positive model that boys can understand and work toward.

insights.claim: Sax claims current American popular culture offers few good role models for young men, so adults must deliberately supply something to aspire to, such as chivalry.
insights.speaker: Leonard Sax

insights.claim: Aaron Renn's IFS essay on why young men are drawn to the manosphere advised against 'appeals to retro concepts and norms' and criticized both Sax and Chris Hatch's viral advice that young men quit video games, get haircuts and shower to be more attractive to women.

insights.so_what: Shows an intra-conservative split on how to address young-male disaffection, a cohort with political and consumer significance.
